Build a feature whose State has a home outside the component.

A detail view is easy to begin and easy to outgrow. As loading, editing, errors, and cleanup arrive, one component can become responsible for user interaction, rendering, and the rules that govern its data. This tutorial starts by giving the character feature a focused State boundary before those responsibilities become tangled.

Why this boundary matters

keeps Feature State and its pipeline in an Angular service, so the component can stay focused on display and temporary user interaction. It does not replace the component; it gives the component a clear, reactive State source to render.

Use this structure for

  • a profile, product, or record detail view
  • a selected item from a managed collection
  • a feature that will later add editing, loading, and validation

By the end of this chapter

You will have a typed, service-owned , initialized with character State and exposed to an Angular component as a read-only, reactive detail view.

The Angular integration includes:

Step 3: Define Feature State
↑ top

State is the feature-owned data that describes a feature at a specific moment. Defining State means deciding which values belong to the feature, assigning a type to each value, and identifying which properties are required.

In TypeScript, an interface captures those decisions as a compile-time contract for the and its consumers. This contract makes the expected State shape explicit, keeps State usage consistent, and allows TypeScript to identify missing properties and incompatible values during development. The interface defines the shape of State; it does not create or load a State value.

In , each declares State for a single Feature. This keeps the State definition focused on the data owned by that Feature instead of combining unrelated application data into one shared global store definition.

In this tutorial, the Feature and its State represent characters from the Star Wars universe.

Each character has an identifier, name, faction, and force-sensitive status. Keeping these fields in one focused State definition gives the , Pipeline, and Angular application a consistent representation of the character data.

Take Action
  1. Create a new file named: star-wars-character.shape.ts 
{{ starWarsCharacterFile().source }}
Global Store vs.

In a global store, all application data is combined into one shared State definition. This can lead to a large, complex State shape that is difficult to manage and maintain. In contrast, a defines State for a single Feature, keeping the State definition focused and manageable.

Step 8: Display Character State
↑ top

This step narrows the tutorial to the UI-facing files that complete the first read path. The service boundary is already in place; now the component, template, and stylesheet turn that registered character collection into a visible detail view.

For , the important separation is simple: the component reads display-ready State, and the service owns the .

In this example, the component reads the service's reactive State, derives one displayed character, and passes only template-ready values to the view. The stylesheet is included here because later tutorial expansions reuse the same presentation base.

What to Look For
